lesson.title: Letting the Numbers Talk: Estimating Limits from Tables
lesson.summary: When a formula resists direct substitution, plugging in numbers that creep closer and closer to the target x-value from both sides often reveals the limit before any algebra does.
lesson.body:
Sometimes a limit needs to be estimated before it can be proven, especially when a formula looks complicated or when a graph is not readily available. A table of values gives numeric teeth to the intuitive limit idea of numbers getting closer and closer: choose x-values that creep toward the target point a, compute f(x) at each one, and watch what number the outputs seem to be approaching. This is often the very first tool reached for on an unfamiliar limit, before any algebraic simplification is attempted, simply because building a table only requires arithmetic, not insight into how an expression might factor or simplify.

Because a two-sided limit only exists when both directions agree, a proper table always straddles the target x-value from both sides. To estimate lim as x approaches 3 of some f(x), compute f at x = 2.9, 2.99, 2.999, approaching from below, and separately at x = 3.1, 3.01, 3.001, approaching from above. The value x = 3 itself is deliberately left out of the table, since that is often exactly the point where the original formula is undefined.

Worked example: estimate lim as x approaches 3 of f(x) = (x^2 - 9) / (x - 3). Plugging x = 3 directly gives 0/0, undefined, which is precisely why a table is a useful first move, alongside or before factoring the expression algebraically. Approaching from below: at x = 2.9, f(2.9) = (8.41 - 9) / (-0.1) = (-0.59) / (-0.1) = 5.9. At x = 2.99, f(2.99) = (8.9401 - 9) / (-0.01) = (-0.0599) / (-0.01) = 5.99. At x = 2.999, the value works out to 5.999. Approaching from above: at x = 3.1, f(3.1) = (9.61 - 9) / (0.1) = 0.61 / 0.1 = 6.1. At x = 3.01, f(3.01) = (9.0601 - 9) / (0.01) = 0.0601 / 0.01 = 6.01. At x = 3.001, the value works out to 6.001. Both sides of the table are converging on 6, so lim as x approaches 3 of f(x) = 6.

This numeric answer matches the algebra exactly. Since x^2 - 9 factors as (x - 3)(x + 3), the expression (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) simplifies to x + 3 for every x except x = 3, where the original form is undefined. The table is really just sampling the line y = x + 3 near x = 3, whose value there would be 3 + 3 = 6, so the numeric pattern in the table is a direct preview of what the algebraic limit technique confirms exactly. Notice too how each row of the table gets closer to 6 by roughly a factor of ten as x gets ten times closer to 3, at 2.9 the value is off by 0.1, at 2.99 it is off by 0.01, and at 2.999 it is off by 0.001, a steady, predictable shrinking that is itself a good sign the table is tracking a genuine limit rather than noise.

Tables are best treated as a way to form a solid conjecture about a limit's value, not as final proof on their own. Not enough decimal precision can hide the true trend, and functions that oscillate rapidly can produce a misleading table depending on exactly which x-values happen to be chosen, a subtlety explored further in the numerical estimation chapter. Whenever possible, confirm a table's suggested limit with an algebraic simplification or a graph before treating it as settled.
